title: Practice Passage 19: The Communication Methods of Cetaceans

passage.title: The Communication Methods of Cetaceans
passage.sub_title: Investigating acoustic signals, toothed whale echolocation, baleen whale songs, ship engine masking, and marine noise policies.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] Cetaceans—the group of marine mammals that includes whales, dolphins, and porpoises—live in an environment where vision is highly limited. [A2] Sunlight penetrates only a few hundred meters beneath the ocean surface, leaving the depths in complete darkness. [A3] Furthermore, water is often cloudy, which restricts visibility even in shallow areas. [A4] Because of these environmental limitations, cetaceans rely on sound rather than sight as their primary method of communication and navigation.

Paragraph B

[B1] Sound travels much faster and farther in water than it does in air, making it an ideal communication medium for ocean life. [B2] Under optimal conditions, low-frequency sounds can travel thousands of kilometers across the ocean. [B3] Cetaceans produce a wide variety of sounds, including clicks, whistles, and complex songs. [B4] These acoustic signals are used to locate prey, maintain social contact, and attract mates.

Paragraph C

[C1] Toothed whales, such as bottlenose dolphins and killer whales, use a highly sophisticated technique called echolocation. [C2] They produce high-frequency clicks that travel through the water and bounce off objects, including fish and geographic features. [C3] By listening to the returning echoes, the animals create a detailed mental map of their surroundings. [C4] Echolocation is so precise that a dolphin can determine the size, shape, and speed of a target from a distance.

Paragraph D

[D1] In contrast, baleen whales, including blue and humpback whales, do not use echolocation. [D2] Instead, they produce low-frequency vocalizations, often referred to as whale songs. [D3] These songs consist of repeating patterns of notes that can last for hours. [D4] Humpback whale songs are particularly complex, and all males in a single population sing the same song, which evolves gradually over time.

Paragraph E

[E1] Ocean noise pollution created by human activity represents a growing threat to cetacean communication. [E2] Large commercial ships produce constant low-frequency noise that overlaps with the frequencies used by baleen whales. [E3] Military sonar systems and offshore drilling operations also generate intense underwater sound waves. [E4] This human-made noise can mask whale calls, making it difficult for animals to find mates or locate their groups.

Paragraph F

[F1] The consequences of noise pollution can be severe. [F2] High-intensity sounds can cause physical damage to whale hearing structures, leading to disorientation and beaching events. [F3] In areas with heavy shipping traffic, some whales have been observed changing the frequency or volume of their calls to be heard over the noise, similar to humans shouting in a crowded room. [F4] However, these behavioral adjustments consume extra energy and may not always prevent communication failure.

Paragraph G

[G1] Protecting the acoustic environment of the oceans is critical for cetacean conservation. [G2] Environmental organizations are advocating for international regulations to reduce ship engine noise. [G3] Restricting military sonar exercises in areas known to be important whale habitats is another key strategy. [G4] Ensuring that the oceans remain quiet enough for marine mammals to communicate is essential for preserving these majestic species.
